notes.claim: Specific heat capacity is how much energy it takes to warm 1 kg by 1 degree, and water's is 4,200 J per kg per degree Celsius.
Seawater has a density of about 1025 kg/m³ and a specific heat of about 3850 J/(kg °C); the numbers used for gravity here are g about 9.8 m/s².
The energy needed to change a material's temperature depends on its mass, its specific heat capacity and the temperature change wanted.
For water, 4,200 J raises 1 kg by 1 °C.
Latent heat is energy that enters or leaves during a phase change without any temperature change, so melting or boiling happens at a steady temperature.
Water's heat of fusion is 334 J/g and its heat of vaporization is 2260 J/g, so boiling away a kilogram takes about 2,260 kJ.
As a cable heats up, heat dissipation increases until it equals the heat generated; the cable is then in thermal equilibrium.
Thermal resistance of a cable's surroundings is the surface temperature rise above ambient divided by the losses per unit length, in K·m/W.
Equal temperature does not mean equal heat flow: metal feels colder than wood because heat leaves your fingers faster.
A motor's heating time constant is typically between 0.5 and 5 hours (added for i2's motor screen).
A protection relay's thermal model comes from the same differential equation for temperature rise caused by current in a conductor (added for i2's motor screen).
For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute (kelvin) temperature.
At constant temperature, halving a fixed amount of gas's volume doubles its pressure.
Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure.
A larger air receiver prevents pressure fluctuation and frequent compressor motor starts.
The atmosphere pushes with about 10^5 Pa, 100 kPa (the weight of 10 m of seawater); 1 bar is 100 kPa (i3, a cited constant).
Cited constant: the specific gas constant of air is 287 J/(kg K), for pV = mRT (i3).
Cited constant: air at sea level has a density of about 1.229 kg/m3, a check on pV = mRT (i3).
A common sizing rule (CAGI): a receiver should give at least 2 minutes of compressor running between cut-in and cut-out, with no air drawn (i3).
A higher receiver pressure does not give more flow: as the pressure is raised, the compressor's flow falls (i3).
A receiver collects condensate and water from the air after the compressor, which has to be drained (i3).
Before work on a compressed air system, isolate it from all pressure sources and vent it completely to atmosphere (HSE HSG39; i3).
A pressure gauge shows that pressure is there but does not prove it has all gone; confirm zero pressure at an open vent before breaking into a system (HSE HSG253; i3).
The first law defines the change in a system's internal energy as the heat transferred into it minus the work it does.
It is impossible to convert all heat from a reservoir into work in a cyclical process that returns the system to its original state.
In a reciprocating engine, the exhaust gas and cooling systems generally carry 60 to 70 percent of the inlet fuel energy.
For large marine two-stroke engines, about half of the fuel energy is lost as waste heat (a 2025 marine paper).
A diesel is a compression ignition engine; it can run a higher compression ratio than a petrol (Otto) engine because only air is compressed, so the fuel cannot ignite early (for i4's diesel outline).
Seawater's specific heat is about 3,850 J per kg per °C (for i4's cooler sum).
Fluid pressure increases with depth because of the weight of the fluid above.
With g about 9.8 m/s² and seawater at 1025 kg/m³, a pressure change of 100 dbar corresponds to a depth change of 99.55 m.
Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
The buoyant force comes from the difference in pressure on the top and bottom of an object.
A submerged object feels a buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces (Archimedes' principle).
Fresh water has a density of about 1000 kg/m³: the kilogram was first the mass of 1000 mL (1 L) of water. Added for i5, whose screens use fresh water at 1000 kg/m³.

Pascal's principle: a change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is passed on undiminished to every part of it and to its walls, which is how a hydraulic jack multiplies force. Added for i5's jack screens.
Relative density (specific gravity) is the ratio of a thing's density to water's. Added for i5, which gives seawater's as 1.025.
For an incompressible fluid, the flow rate is the same everywhere along the pipe, so it must speed up where the pipe narrows.
When a fluid flows into a narrower channel its speed and kinetic energy increase, and the energy has to come from somewhere: the pressure.
Venturi flow meters work on Bernoulli's principle, using the pressure difference between the pipe and its narrowing to measure flow.
The transition from laminar to turbulent flow is put at Reynolds numbers between about 2000 and 10 000, so its upper edge is contested.
Pitot tubes, venturi meters and orifice plates are used to measure pressure and flow speed.
A sharp-edged orifice has coefficients of velocity, contraction and discharge (Cv, Cc, Cd).
Head is the height to which a pump can raise a liquid, measured in metres.
Friction loss in a system depends on the length and size of the pipework, bends and valves.
In turbulent pipe flow, resistance to flow is proportional to the square of the mean flow velocity.
Pump power in kW is flow times head times specific gravity divided by 367.46 times efficiency, with flow in m³/h and head in metres.
The motor's electrical input power is higher than the pump's shaft power, by the motor's own efficiency.

A U-tube manometer is a tube part-filled with liquid, one leg joined to the pressure and the other open to the air; the difference in the liquid levels represents the pressure (added for i7's gauges, review fix).
A Bourdon gauge's flattened tube, bent into a C, tends to straighten as it is pressurised, and that movement drives its needle (added for i7's gauges, review fix).
A Bourdon gauge reads gauge pressure, relative to the atmosphere around it (added for i7's gauges, review fix).
A centrifugal pump settles at the operating point, where its curve of head against flow crosses the system's curve.
Closing a discharge valve changes the system resistance curve.
With the discharge valve closed, a centrifugal pump builds maximum head, and the power the motor needs is at or near its minimum.
As the valve opens and flow rises, the motor's current rises (source is a pump maker's start-up guide; it covers centrifugal pumps generally).
Net positive suction head (NPSH) is the minimum absolute suction pressure needed to avoid cavitation.
Cavitation is usually unwanted because of its noise and the damage it does to blade surfaces, such as pitting.
Positive displacement pumps are normally fitted with relief valves ahead of their discharge valves, to protect the pump and its discharge pipe from overpressure.
Water boils at 100 °C at sea-level pressure, and at a lower temperature where the pressure is lower.
